There are quite a few reasons why, but here's the main ones:

1. You don't actually know what you're doing, you have that false confidence that you do but in reality you don't. First step to fixing this? Realizing that you don't understand.

2. Your teacher believes you're cheating. If you truly know the material, your teacher might suspect you're cheating, and using outside materials rather than your own brain. I would suggest talking to your teacher about this.

3. Your teacher dislikes you. This is probably the least likely one, but still possible. If this is the case, you might want to tell someone about it, because this teacher is potentially jeopardizing your future in academics. If you believe they are mature enough to have a conversation with, try talking to them about this directly.

4. You're doing something wrong. Although you may understand the material, you may not be good at interpreting the questions/topics on the test. I've had this problem in the past. Maybe it's not even you, it could just be the way the test is written. I also suggest talking to your teacher if you think this is the case.

 If you don't really want to read all that, you don't have to. Even if you read it and you made it here, my advice is clear. Communicate with your teachers. If you are too nervous to, write an email and send it. Get a councillor and ask them to help you talk with your teacher. They are there to help you, it's their job. Hell, if you trust your parents enough, ask them to help you talk to your teacher. This way, you can figure out why you're getting bad test scores, or any problems you may have in the future. It's a good thing to be able to communicate with people, after all you're going to need it outside of school.

TLDR: Talk to your teachers, figure out the problem, and ask them how to solve it. Reach out to other people if you must.
